name: Diego Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a loader underground, what we call a bogger, at the Kessler copper mine outside Millbrook. We go down the ramp at six, I pick up broken rock from the drawpoints after the blast and tip it into the ore pass, back and forth for ten hours. It's hot down there, about 30 degrees at 1,100 metres, and the noise never stops. I like that every shift is a bit different, because the rock is never the same.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's around you down there, and what's life like outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: There's about twelve of us on my crew, and my shift boss Rangi is fair but strict about safety. A couple of the loaders on level 9 are already run by remote from a room on the surface, which we joke is the air-conditioned future. I rent a house with my mate Karim, who's an electrician on another crew. I've got about four months of bills saved, and I send my mum a bit each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, there you go, all that noise for not much. At work we'd joke that the remote loaders still need a person in the chair. I'd probably post something about spending the money on mine safety instead of hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my job looks about the same, which is fine by me. The remote loaders on level 9 would keep spreading slowly, but they still need operators. I'd want one of those chairs eventually, once I've seen how it goes for the guys who moved up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and keep saving about 500 a month. I'd put my name down for the tele-remote course when it opens next year, because it's proven now and the pay is the same. I'd stay in the union, mostly turning up and voting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, honestly. My job's steady, the pay's fine, and I've got a bit put away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want one of those surface chairs. What's holding you back now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to see how it goes for Mateo first, he's the guy from my crew who moved up to the remote room in March. He says the screens gave him headaches for the first month and then it was fine. I'm not the first one through the door, but I'm usually the second, once I've seen nobody got hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything outside AI that worries you about the next few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Copper prices, a bit, because when prices drop they cut contractors first. But I'm on staff, so I'd be fine unless it got really bad. Rent's gone up twice in Millbrook, that's the main thing.

say: I'd joke that the **remote loaders** still need someone in the chair.
I'd post that the money should go to **mine safety** instead of hype.
think: My job stays **about the same**, which suits me fine.
I'd want a **surface chair** eventually, once I've seen how others manage.
do: Keep my shifts and save about **500 a month**.
Sign up for the **tele-remote course** when it opens next year.
Keep turning up and voting at **union meetings**.
feel: Pretty **calm**, because my job is **steady** and I have savings.
S0.quote: I'm not the first one through the door, but I'm usually the second, once I've seen nobody got hurt.
fieldNote: He calls himself the **second one** through the door, never the first.
His main pressure is **rising rent** in Millbrook, not AI.
He watches a crew mate's **move to remote** work before deciding his own.

steps.text: Keep working the Kessler loader shifts as normal
Sign up for next year's tele-remote loader course
Save about 500 a month into the bank

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: the office jobs get hit first, and we underground lot get a few more years. I'd say the union should be at the table now, not after the first round of cuts. Online I'd share posts about the government funding retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think Rangi's paperwork, the shift plans and the ore tracking, would mostly go to software, and the planning office would shrink. For me, the remote room grows faster, so the choice is move up to a screen or stay in the dark until they don't need me. I'd move up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the tele-remote course in the first six months instead of waiting. I'd start using the AI chat app on my phone more, to check the mine's safety procedures and help with the course notes. And I'd push the union for a deal that surface jobs go to current crews first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly for other people. For me it feels like a ladder showing up, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planners, honestly, and Leila in the stores office, who orders everything from drill bits to toilet paper. Her job is buying and booking, which is exactly the list. I go down a ramp a kilometre underground every day, and somehow the woman ordering our drill bits is in more danger than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Karim see it the same way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Karim thinks electricians are safe forever, because someone has to wire the robots. I tell him that's what the loader drivers said about the remote room. We argue about it over dinner most nights.

say: I'd say **office jobs** get hit first and underground crews get a few more years.
I'd say the union must be **at the table** before the first cuts.
think: Shift plans and **ore tracking** go to software, so the planning office shrinks.
The **remote room** grows, so I'd move up to a screen rather than wait.
do: Do the **tele-remote course** in the first six months.
Use the **AI chat app** on my phone for procedures and course notes.
Push the union for **surface jobs** to go to current crews first.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, mostly for others, because it feels like a **ladder**, not a cliff.
S1.quote: I go down a ramp a kilometre underground every day, and somehow the woman ordering our drill bits is in more danger than me.
fieldNote: He sees the **stores office** as more exposed than his underground job, and finds that strange.
His steady style speeds up here: he'd **stop waiting** for proof.
He frames union action as protecting **current crews**' first claim on new jobs.

steps.text: Finish the tele-remote loader course within six months
Use the AI chat app to study mine safety procedures
Push the union for surface jobs to go to current crews

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a real safety net, like a basic income or a jobs guarantee, because no retraining scheme moves that fast. I'd say it at the union and I'd say it online. I'd also say the mining companies should pay for it, since they'll save the most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the remote room is just a waiting room. If AI can do any thinking by 2028, the person in the remote chair is the first thing it replaces, and then robots do the hands-on bits by 2031. So the ladder I was counting on gets pulled up before I've climbed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd stop the extra I send my mum and tell her why, which would be a hard call. I'd go from 500 to 900 a month in savings by selling the car and taking the mine bus. I'd look at the electrical apprenticeship with Karim, because fixing robots in tight underground spaces might last past 2031. And I'd go to every union meeting and every rally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the first time I'd feel like being the second one through the door is too slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only 2 years of warning change, compared with the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, there's no time to wait and watch, which is how I always do things. My whole plan was to let someone else go first and then follow, and with two years there's nobody ahead of me to follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell your mum about stopping the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call her on a Sunday, she likes Sundays. I'd say it's for a year, while I work out what's next. She'd say she'll manage, and she'd cut her own groceries, which makes me feel worse.

say: I'd call for a **basic income** or jobs guarantee, because retraining can't move that fast.
I'd say **mining companies** should pay, since they'll save the most.
think: The **remote chair** is the first job thinking AI replaces in 2028.
Robots by **2031** pull the ladder up before I've climbed it.
do: Stop the **money to my mum** for a year and explain why.
Raise savings to **900 a month** by selling the car.
Look at an **electrical apprenticeship** to fix robots underground.
feel: **Alarmed**, because waiting to be **second** is suddenly too slow.
S2.quote: My whole plan was to let someone else go first and then follow, and with two years there's nobody ahead of me to follow.
fieldNote: His usual **wait-and-watch** approach breaks down with only two years.
Cutting money to his **mother** is the hardest call he names.
He shifts to calls for a **basic income**, saying training can't keep up.

steps.text: Pause the monthly money sent to Mum for a year
Sell the car and save 900 a month
Apply for an electrical apprenticeship alongside Karim
Attend every union meeting and rally for a safety net

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable, if the government starts now. I'd say every mine should publish its automation plan so crews know where they stand. I'd say that at the union and post it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think five years gets me through the electrical apprenticeship with a bit to spare before robots in 2034. The remote room stops being the safe bet, because AGI takes the screen work in 2031. So I'd skip the screen and go straight to the hands that fix the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the electrical apprenticeship in the second year, after saving a cushion of about eight months first. I'd keep sending my mum money but less, 100 instead of 200. I'd ask Rangi to put me on the crew that installs the remote gear, to learn it on the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. It's the same worry as the fast one, with time to do something about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait a year to start the apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Apprentice pay is about half what I earn now, and rent in Millbrook isn't getting cheaper. I'd rather save eight months of rent first than start an apprenticeship and quit halfway because I can't pay the landlord.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the 3-year gap between thinking AI and robots mean for a job like yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job is nearly all hands and eyes, so the thinking AI barely touches the actual loading. It changes who tells me where to go and what to load, the planning and dispatch. The robots are what finish my job, so those three years are my real deadline.

say: I'd say **five years** is workable if government **starts now**.
I'd say every mine should publish its **automation plan** for crews.
think: Five years gets me through an **electrical apprenticeship** before robots in 2034.
The **remote room** stops being safe, because AGI takes screen work in 2031.
do: Save an **eight-month cushion** before starting the apprenticeship in year two.
Cut money to my mum from **200 to 100** a month.
Ask Rangi for the crew that **installs remote gear**.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a **plan** and time to act.
S3.quote: I'd rather save eight months of rent first than start an apprenticeship and quit halfway because I can't pay the landlord.
fieldNote: He'd **skip the screen job** entirely and train to fix machines.
He sees the **three-year robot gap** as his real deadline, not the AGI date.
**Apprentice pay** at half his wage shapes his timing.

steps.text: Build an eight-month rent cushion before switching
Start the electrical apprenticeship in year two
Cut money sent to Mum from 200 to 100

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty to do it fairly, so there's no excuse. I'd say mines should train their own people for the new jobs, and the union should hold them to it. I'd be the one at the barbecue saying calm down, we've got time, but use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years suits how I am. I can watch the early people move, then follow when it's proven, like I always do. Robots by 2039 means I'm thirty-nine, which is fine if I've already switched by thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep loading and saving 500 a month for the first few years. I'd do the tele-remote course anyway because it's cheap and useful, and plan an apprenticeship around 2029. Maybe I'd look at buying a small place in Millbrook with Karim instead of renting, because the job's safe long enough for a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. Uneasy at the edges, the way you feel about something you know is coming but not yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd consider a mortgage. Isn't that a risk if the job ends in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but a small place paid down for ten years is better than ten more years of rising rent. If I've got ten years of loader wages ahead of me, I'd rather pay off bricks than pay off a landlord.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first sign that would make you move earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the remote room starts hiring fewer people instead of more, that's it. Mateo would tell me before anyone, he hears the gossip up there. Then I'd stop waiting.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty, so there's **no excuse** for unfairness.
I'd say mines should **train their own people** for new jobs.
think: Ten years suits me, because I can **follow once proven**.
Robots by **2039** are fine if I've switched by thirty-two.
do: Keep loading and saving **500 a month** for a few years.
Take the **tele-remote course** now and plan an apprenticeship for 2029.
Look at **buying a small place** in Millbrook with Karim.
S4.quote: If I've got ten years of loader wages ahead of me, I'd rather pay off bricks than pay off a landlord.
fieldNote: More time fits his **follow-when-proven** habit almost perfectly.
He'd **take on a mortgage**, betting the job lasts ten years.
His early warning sign is the **remote room** hiring fewer people.

steps.text: Keep running the underground loader at Kessler as normal
Take the tele-remote course and plan a 2029 apprenticeship
Buy a small house in Millbrook with Karim
Save 500 a month toward the house deposit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes away the thing I'm good at, which is waiting to see. What would help is some income while I retrain, not just a course with no pay. Something like apprentice wages topped up by the government.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the guys who've been underground twenty years. A lot of the older miners can't read a screen without their glasses, and nobody's writing a plan for them.

headlineQuote: A lot of the older miners can't read a screen without their glasses, and nobody's writing a plan for them.
portrait: Diego, 27, drives an **underground loader** at the Kessler copper mine near Millbrook.
He rents with his friend Karim, has about **four months** saved and helps his **mum**.
He's pro-union and **progressive**, and backs a safety net over retraining alone.
He's the **second one** through the door, moving once he's seen change work.
With **two years** of warning his wait-and-watch habit fails, and he becomes alarmed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it leaves no time to watch others go first.
whatWouldHelp: Government-topped **apprentice wages**, so he has income while he retrains.
